title: Cardinals stun Chargers as offense struggles in Mike McDaniel’s debut as L.A.’s OC
content:
INGLEWOOD, Calif. — The Arizona Cardinals upset the Los Angeles Chargers 26-14 on Sunday at SoFi Stadium.

The teams traded rushing touchdowns in the first quarter, with rookie running back Jeremiyah Love notching the first score of his NFL career. With a chance to tie at 10 with two minutes left in the first half, Jim Harbaugh chose to go for it on fourth-and-goal from the Cardinals’ 3-yard line. The result was a sack of Justin Herbert and the Cardinals marched down for a field goal and a 13-7 halftime lead.

It was special teams that stepped up for Arizona in the fourth quarter, when Simi Fehoko blocked a JK Scott punt and it was recovered at the Chargers’ 3-yard line with 12:28 remaining. That set up a Jacoby Brissett touchdown pass to Trey McBride for a 23-14 lead. Andrew Wingard’s interception of Herbert on the ensuing drive essentially sealed the win for the Cardinals.

Box score | Week 1 live blog | Game discussion

It certainly looked like it. Entering Mike LaFleur’s first season as head coach, the Cardinals were expected to be among the NFL’s worst teams, if not the worst. The Athletic’s Austin Mock projected 4.4 wins, the fewest in the NFL. Given Arizona’s schedule, which looks difficult, that sounded about right.

Then came Sunday. It’s one game, but this at least changes the conversation and gives pause to those writing off the Cardinals. Maybe that lasts only a week or two, but it’s safe to say Arizona was a Week 1 surprise. Brissett showed why teammates like playing with him so much — he doesn’t lock onto one receiver and spreads the ball around. Six receivers had catches, and three of them (McBride, Kendrick Bourne and Michael Wilson) had at least five.

Then there was the defense. GM Monti Ossenfort did little to upgrade a beat-up unit that fell apart during the second half of last season, betting that better health would lead to improvement. The Cardinals weren’t great Sunday — the pass rush was mostly non-existent in the first half — but it made plays when it mattered. Defensive lineman Dante Stills had a huge fourth-down stop near the goal line. The Cardinals also forced two turnovers, blocked a punt and blanked the Chargers in the fourth quarter.

LaFleur, though, wasn’t interested in discussing expectations for his team.

“For this team, what’s been said, it doesn’t matter,” he told reporters after the game. “We don’t care. And I hope we continue to feel that way. I just told them: Humility is a day away in this league. We got to reset and get back to work, but I’m happy for those guys.”

An impressive, unexpected start, for sure. — Doug Haller

So much for a quick fix. For all of the anticipation of an explosive new offensive attack sparked by the arrival of new coordinator Mike McDaniel, the Chargers stumbled and fumbled their way through their season debut. Those struggles largely cost Los Angeles its first victory of the season. Turnovers, third-down struggles and a sputtering rushing attack resulted in a lack of sustained drives, a feeble attack and an embarrassing defeat.

Last season, the Chargers ranked 12th in offensive yards (333.8 per game) but 19th in points (21.6). Third downs represented a strength as L.A. converted 45.8 percent of them into first downs (third-best in the league). McDaniel and head coach Jim Harbaugh described themselves as the perfect match, and McDaniel has praised Herbert’s abilities while expressing excitement over how he will be able to use the quarterback. However, the improvement Harbaugh sought when he hired McDaniel now appears likely to take some time to develop.

Herbert and his teammates did deliver an impressive first series — a crisp, eight-play, 77-yard scoring drive capped by an Omarion Hampton touchdown run. But from there, the Chargers managed only one scoring drive for the remainder of the game.

Outside of Ladd McConkey, who had five catches for 82 yards and a touchdown on seven targets, and tight end David Njoku (five catches on five targets for 58 yards), Herbert struggled to connect with his pass catchers, and a rushing attack that averaged just 3.8 yards per carry provided little support.

The struggles didn’t reflect a ferocious Cardinals defensive effort. Instead, the Chargers’ wounds were largely self-inflicted. Hampton fumbled across midfield on their second possession. Harbaugh opted against a chip-shot field goal from the Arizona 3 late in the second quarter and Herbert was sacked for a turnover on downs. A brief reprieve on the second possession of the third quarter delivered the second touchdown of the day, but from there, L.A. failed to develop any rhythm.

McConkey left the game with a chest injury in the fourth quarter, and without his top weapon, Herbert couldn’t rally his unit for a comeback. In fact, the Chargers didn’t cross midfield at all in the second half aside from the one scoring drive. — Mike Jones

Among Arizona’s biggest storylines will be how it manages the workload of No. 3 pick Love. The safe move — and maybe the right one — is to be cautious. The Cardinals have learned as much. They lost Love for the bulk of the preseason after he sprained an ankle on his 14th touch against the Las Vegas Raiders. Leading up to Sunday’s game, Love said the recovery process has been difficult, simply because he wanted to get back on the field.

But here’s the thing: Love at times was the most explosive player on the field against the Chargers. It wasn’t reflected in his overall numbers, just in select plays — the 5-yard touchdown run on Arizona’s first possession and the 18-yard rush that led to a Chad Ryland field goal.

“That first touchdown, I thought you saw (Love’s) explosiveness,” LaFleur said. “I expect him to get better and better. He hasn’t practiced in three or four weeks (because of the ankle sprain) and he’s just going to get more and more conditioned out there.”

Love finished with 13 touches for 50 total yards. In the fourth quarter, Arizona rode Tyler Allgeier to finish off the Chargers. It was an effective approach, but as the season unfolds, Love might be difficult to take off the field. — Haller
